title: The true person
hookLine: the untrue person boasts of family and learning; the true person just practices
last: EACH PIECE IS SMALL AND PASSING.

lines: THE TRUE PERSON, AND THE UNTRUE.
cards: Some groups have one: the person who mentions, early on, where they went to school. Or how long they've been coming. Or that they read the book in the original.

Sometimes, honestly, it's us. The hundred and thirteenth discourse is the Buddha's portrait of exactly this, set among monks, where it might seem least likely. It's called the discourse on the true person.
And the untrue person in it isn't lazy or wicked. He's often quite accomplished.

teach.b: The Pali word is sappurisa, a good, true person, and the Buddha builds it by contrast. Here's an untrue person.
He went forth from a high-ranking family, so he praises himself and looks down on others: I'm from a noble family; these other monks aren't. The list goes on. A wealthy family.
Well-known. Plenty of robes and food. Learned.
An expert in the discipline. A gifted teacher. Lives in the forest.
Wears rag robes. Eats once a day.
Each time, the same move: I have this, they don't. It even reaches the deep meditative absorptions: an untrue person can reach real stillness and boast about that too. Now the true person.
Same family, same learning, same forest hut.
But he reflects: greed, hatred and delusion aren't destroyed by being from a noble family. Someone from an ordinary family who practices the teaching well is worthy of honor.
So he puts the practice first. He doesn't praise himself or look down on others. With the absorptions, the text goes further: he doesn't even build an identity out of them.
Whatever he imagines a state to be, it's already otherwise. Notice what the Buddha doesn't say. Good families, learning and forest life aren't bad.
The test isn't what you have. It's what you do with it in the room: lift yourself, or just practice.

how: In Buddhist monasteries seniority is counted by years since ordination, not by family, wealth or learning, and teachers in several traditions warn students against comparing themselves with others over meditative attainments.

o: a true person, who doesn't lift himself over others
a monk who has mastered every rule of discipline
a person born into a noble, high-ranking family

games.q: true and untrue: tap the pairs.
p: praises himself, looks down on others

s: MN 113 says good families and learning are bad
it says they don't end greed, hatred and delusion; what matters is practice and not boasting.
the untrue person in MN 113 can reach deep meditative states
the list reaches the absorptions: even real stillness can become something to boast about.
the true person, in the text, refuses to live in the forest
he may live in the forest too; he just doesn't use it to lift himself above others.

games.q: you're a monk from a noble family, sitting with monks who aren't. what does the true person reflect, according to MN 113?
o: my family gives me a head start.
greed and hatred aren't ended by family; practice is what counts.
I should hide where I come from.
games.why: the true person sees that family doesn't destroy greed, hatred or delusion, and honors anyone who practices well.

practice: Think of one thing you're quietly proud of, a degree, a skill, years of practice, a streak, and notice whether there's a little lift in it, an I have this. No need to scold it.
Set it down beside you, and come back to the breath, which doesn't care about any of it.

wordCard.voice: Sappurisa. A good, true person: one who has family, learning or deep practice, and still doesn't praise himself or look down on others.

orig.note: Pali sappurisa: a good, true person. MN 113 sets it against asappurisa, the untrue person.

carryVoice: Your line: no boast. What you have matters less than what you do with it. Until tomorrow.
